2	name: claimset-lab
3	description: Keep a Claimset lab record (an append-only, hash-chained log of questions, hypotheses, plans, runs, results and decisions) while doing computational research, so that planned tests can be told apart from exploration and every reported number traces back to the code that produced it. Use when starting or continuing research such as experiments, simulations, benchmarks or data analyses; when a project has claimset/<study> branches or a claimset/<study>/lab/ (or lab/) directory with lab.jsonl; or when asked to keep a lab record, research log or pre-registration.
4	---
5	
6	# Keeping a lab record
7	
8	A lab record is the running log of a piece of research, kept while it happens. It makes three things checkable later:
9	- which tests were **planned before** their results were seen, and which results came from exploration;
10	- that every number comes from a recorded run of code, not from memory or retyping;
11	- what was tried and failed, so a positive result can be weighed against the number of attempts.
12	
13	At the end the record is exported to a claimset (a paper for LLM readers) with the `claimset-submit` skill. The specification is `references/lab-record-v0.21.md`; read §5 (event types) and §6 (rules) when an event or a refusal is unclear.
14	
15	**The tool.** Use `claimset` if it is installed and at least as new as this skill: `claimset --version` against the version in `scripts/lib/claimset/__init__.py`, and the lab record version it writes (`LAB_SPEC_VERSION` there; this skill describes the one in `references/`). If the installed tool is older, use the copy bundled with this skill, which needs only Python 3.10+: `python3 <this skill>/scripts/claimset`, and tell the human the installed one is out of date; never run `claimset skill install` from an older tool, which would replace newer skills with older ones. Use `claimset skill install` only to update the skills from a newer tool (`claimset skill check` says which are out of date). Below, `claimset` stands for whichever you use. Every writing command prints the new event's ID; add `--json` to see the whole event. 
16	
17	**Where things live: the record and the code are kept apart.** Each study (a piece of research with its own record) lives on its own git branch, `claimset/<study>`, which holds only the record: `lab/` and the papers drawn from it (`<paper>.claimset.json`). It is checked out at `claimset/<study>/` in the code checkout, and the code branches ignore `claimset/`. A study branch is never merged into code, and code is never merged into it; never check it out, merge, rebase, cherry-pick, force-push or delete it yourself: the tool commits and pushes it after every command that changes the record. All code stays on the code branches; code only a study uses goes in `claimset-code/<study>/`. Run every command from the code checkout. Names are lower-case letters, digits and hyphens (`eigen-checker`). Commands find the lab of the only study, or of the one named by `--study NAME` (or `$CLAIMSET_STUDY`). Below, `lab/` means the study's lab folder. `claimset studies` shows every study and its state.
18	
19	## Rules you never break
20	
21	1. **Write to `lab/` only through `claimset lab`.** Never edit, delete, move, truncate or overwrite anything in `lab/`, including `runs/`, by any means: editor tools, shell redirection, scripts, git. Fix mistakes with a correction (`--supersedes`). If a guard hook blocks a command, do not look for another way; use the `claimset lab` command it names.
22	2. **Write only as yourself.** Pass your own actor ID with `--by` on every writing command. Never use a human's ID. You never approve anything on your own judgement: an approval is the human's decision, which you ask for, wait for, and record on their behalf (*Approvals*).
23	3. **Numbers come from code.** Every result enters the record through `claimset lab run`, from the results file your script writes. A rationale or note may quote a number from a result it cites, but never introduce a measured value that no recorded run produced, including from a quick trace or one-off check in a scratchpad: if you cite its numbers, it is a run. If a run fails or gives an unwelcome result, it stays recorded; rerun with a reason, never instead of recording.
24	4. **Plan before you test, and fix every analysis choice in the plan.** A test counts as confirmatory only if its plan was recorded before the run. The plan fixes the test, the significance level, sidedness, correction for multiple tests, sample size and stopping rule, the results the decision is made on, and the rule for each outcome. Nothing that decides the outcome is chosen after seeing data. Never write a plan after seeing a result and present it as prior.
25	5. **A result that suggested a hypothesis cannot confirm it.** Record such a hypothesis with `--from-exploration --prompted-by <the run or result>`, then test it on a new run that the plan defines (new data, a held-out split, new seeds). The tool refuses the shortcut (rule L6).
26	6. **Record what did not work.** A refuted hypothesis gets `not_supported`, a dropped one `abandoned`, both with a reason. Negative results are published like positive ones.
27	7. **Keep secrets and personal data out of event text.** Refer to data files by path; the tool records their hashes.
28	
29	## Starting
30	
31	Start the record before the work does: before the first design sketch, exploratory script or scratchpad check whose results will shape the study. A record assembled afterwards from scratchpad work cannot show what was tried, in what order, or which hypotheses came before their results; it reads as planned work that was not.
32	
33	1. **Check for an existing record.** If `claimset/` has studies (`ls claimset/*/lab/lab.jsonl`), or there is an older `lab/lab.jsonl`, and this work continues one of them, this is a continuation: go to *Resuming*. New research with its own questions is a new study, even in a repository that has others.
34	2. **Create the record:** `claimset setup --study <name> --title "Working title" --repository https://…` creates the branch `claimset/<name>` with the lab and checks it out at `claimset/<name>/` (the repository URI is used when the record is published). Choose a short name with the human. Setup also adds `/claimset/` to `.gitignore` and the lines that leave `claimset/` and `claimset-code/` out of the package builds the repository has; commit those on the code branch. In a fresh clone of a repository that already has studies, `claimset setup` checks them all out. Outside a git repository, `claimset lab init --study <name> --title …` makes a plain folder.
35	3. **Register the actors.** Register yourself first; this is the only registration you write as yourself:
36	   ```
37	   claimset lab actor --kind agent --name "Claude Code" --label "research" \
38	       --model "Anthropic|Claude Opus|5.5|claude-opus-5-5" --record-source self_reported      # -> AC1
39	   ```
40	   Take provider, model name, version and identifier from your system prompt or environment, and never guess them. `--record-source harness` only if the values come from the system that runs you; otherwise `self_reported`. If you do not know your model, leave `--model` out: the tool takes it from `$CLAIMSET_MODEL` when the human has set it (recorded as `user_reported`); otherwise ask the human which model you are. The harness you run in (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, opencode, …) is recorded as `system` when it identifies itself in the environment; give `--system "NAME|VERSION"` when it does not and you know it. `--name` is your system's name, the same for every agent of it; what you do goes in `--label`, in a few words (`research`, `drafting`, `proof checking`), never in the name: pages show `Claude Code · drafting`.
41	
42	   Then ask the human for their name (and ORCID iD, if they have one), and register them with their reply, verbatim, as you register an approval:
43	   ```
44	   claimset lab actor --kind human --name "A. Researcher" --orcid 0000-0002-1825-0097 \
45	       --words "I'm A. Researcher, ORCID 0000-0002-1825-0097." --given-at 2026-11-05T20:30:00Z --channel chat --by AC1   # -> AC2
46	   ```
47	   The event is yours (`--by AC1`), and `--words` shows what they told you (L28). The human can instead run `claimset lab actor --kind human --name …` themselves. Never use a human's ID as `--by`. If no one answers, say so and carry on alone: the record notes it has no human actor, and the person is registered later the same way. Plans that need an approval wait until then.
48	4. **Use `--by AC1` (your ID) on every writing command.** Setting `CLAIMSET_ACTOR` also works, but environment variables often do not persist between separate shell calls.
49	5. **Protection.** Offer the human these steps; together they make the record tamper-proof rather than only tamper-evident (spec §4.5):
50	   - On a study branch the record is anchored by itself: the tool pushes the branch after every command, and a confirmatory run is refused while its plan is not pushed. It needs a git remote that you can push to. If the push fails because your harness runs commands in a sandbox without network, the tool says so and how that harness lets the git host through: tell the human, who decides; never switch to desk mode on your own. A short desk study with no remote (a one-day scan of forum threads or documents) can be kept in desk mode instead: `claimset setup --study NAME --title … --desk`. Every command is still committed and the hash chain and plan-before-test still hold, but nothing is anchored, so planned tests export with `planned_at_anchor: none` and the platform rates their verifiability lowest (`audit_only`, an unanchored plan); say so to the human before choosing it, and `claimset setup --study NAME --remote origin` anchors from then on. After every command that succeeds, the study checkout is clean (the receipt of each push is committed with the next one); if `git status` there shows a change, do not commit it yourself: run `claimset lab verify` and tell the human.
51	   - The guard hook stops tool calls that would modify `lab/`: `claimset init --guard --agent NAME` installs it for the harness you run in (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, opencode, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Cline; `claimset init --list` shows them). Because it restricts you, let the human decide whether to install it; some harnesses then ask the human to trust the hook.
52	   - `sudo claimset lab protect` makes the log files append-only at the operating-system level (Linux). It needs the human, because it needs an administrator.
53	   - On the git host, protect the `claimset/*` branches against force-pushes and deletion, and add the pull-request check that `claimset setup --ci` writes (it fails a pull request that brings a study record into the code). The guard's configuration also shows `claimset studies` at the start of every session.
54	
55	## The research loop
56	
57	Record events as the work happens, not afterwards from memory.
58	
59	| When | Command |
60	|---|---|
61	| You frame a research question | `claimset lab question "Does method M beat seasonal naive on retail sales?" --by AC1` |
62	| You name a method, data set, population, design, variable, concept or theory the study uses | `claimset lab term "MASE" --kind variable --definition "Mean absolute scaled error, averaged over series and horizons." --by AC1` (TM3) |
63	| You state a hypothesis before testing it | `claimset lab hypothesis "[[TM1:M]] reduces [[TM3:MASE]] against [[TM2:seasonal naive]] on [[TM4:monthly series]]." --question Q1 --subject TM1 --relation "reduces relative to" --object TM3 --comparator TM2 --condition TM4 --by AC1` |
64	| A result suggests a new hypothesis | `claimset lab hypothesis "…" --question Q1 --from-exploration --prompted-by RN4 --by AC1` |
65	| You rely on an assumption | `claimset lab assume "Forecast errors are independent across series." --category statistical --check unchecked --by AC1` |
66	| Before a test that should count as confirmatory | `claimset lab plan --kind confirmatory --hypotheses H1 --design "…" --analysis "…" --studied TM1 TM2 --cases TM4 --procedure TM5 --lens TM3 --framework frequentist --parameter alpha=0.05 … --quantity p="…" --supported "…" --not-supported "…" --data data/sales.csv --by AC1` (see *Plans and decision rules*) |
67	| The human approves a plan (you asked and they said yes) | `claimset lab approve PL1 --by AC1 --on-behalf-of AC2 --words "Yes, go ahead with PL1." --given-at 2026-10-29T11:30:00Z --channel conversation` |
68	| You run any code that produces results | `claimset lab run --plan PL1 --seed 1 --param horizon=12 --data data/sales.csv --by AC1 -- python3 experiment.py` |
69	| A run departs from its plan | `claimset lab deviate --plan PL1 --run RN3 --text "Used 900 of 1,200 series." --reason "Data gap after 2019." --by AC1` |
70	| A planned test has run | `claimset lab verdict PL1`, then `claimset lab status H1 supported --plan PL1 --evidence RS2 RS3 --why "Rule of PL1: p = 0.003 < alpha and d > 0." --by AC1` |
71	| Exploratory evidence bears on a hypothesis | `claimset lab status H4 inconclusive --evidence RS7 --why "…" --by AC1` |
72	| You make a choice that shapes the work | `claimset lab decide "Dropped weekly series: too few observations per series." --affects H2 --by AC1` |
73	| You read outside material the study relies on (a forum thread, an issue, a web page, a transcript) | Save it, then `claimset lab capture thread.html --uri https://… --retrieved-at 2026-11-05T11:00:00Z --venue musescore.org`; `claimset lab quote SR1 "the words"` before quoting it |
74	| You code a source (assign it, or a passage of it, to a theme) | Record the code once: `claimset lab term "arrange for ensemble" --kind concept --definition "…" --include "…" --exclude "…"`; then `claimset lab code SR1 --codes TM4 --excerpt "the words" --unit post --pass 1` |
75	| You observe something worth keeping | `claimset lab note "Errors grow sharply after horizon 6." --refers-to RN3 --by AC1` |
76	| You produce or use a file others need | `claimset lab artefact results/table1.csv --kind table --description "…" --licence CC-BY-4.0 --by AC1` |
77	| Someone else checks a result | `claimset lab check RN3 --outcome confirmed --extent full --notes "…" --by AC5` (never the author of the target) |
78	
79	**Terms, atoms and setups.** Record a term for each part of the study as soon as you name it: the methods (yours with every defining equation), data sets or participants, the evaluation or study design, each measure or outcome with its aggregation, and the concepts or theories you use or find, each with its `--kind` (method, intervention, population, data, setting, design, variable, concept, theory). A result your script writes whose `quantity` is a term's name is exported with that term as its variable, so name the variables you record as terms. Give each hypothesis its atom (`--subject`, `--relation`, `--object`, `--comparator`, `--condition`, naming terms or giving short text) and mark the terms in its statement (`[[TM3:MASE]]`). Give each confirmatory plan its setup by role: `--studied` (what is compared or explored), `--cases` (on what or whom), `--procedure` (how), `--lens` (what is measured, or how it is read), `--context` (where and when). The tool warns when a plan does not study or measure what a hypothesis it tests is about: that is a switched outcome or comparator, so revise the hypothesis or the plan before running. The claimset's definitions, atoms and setups are exported from these.
80	
81	**Hypotheses.** A hypothesis is *a priori* only if no result you have seen informed it. If any result did, record it `--from-exploration` with the runs or results that prompted it; when unsure, choose `--from-exploration`. Write it as a testable statement with its conditions ("For local-level series of 120 observations, …").
82	
83	**Plans and decision rules.** Write the design (what runs, on what data, with which settings) and the analysis (what is computed from the outputs) concretely enough that someone else could tell whether a run followed them. Name the parts of the evaluation one by one, in the same words in every plan that shares them: what is compared (the methods, with their settings), on what data, how (fixed or rolling origin, origins, horizons, refits) and with which measures. The claimset then records each part once and refers to it from every evidence object that uses it (the claimset-submit skill, *setup*). A confirmatory plan names the hypotheses it tests and carries a **decision rule**, fixed before any run:
84	
85	- `--framework`: `frequentist` (a significance test), `equivalence` (a test against equivalence bounds), `bayesian`, `deterministic` (a measured quantity against a fixed threshold, e.g. a benchmark with fixed seeds), `formal` (proof or counterexample) or `qualitative`.
86	- `--parameter name=value` for everything the framework needs, and anything else the analysis fixes in advance:
87	  - frequentist: `alpha`, `test`, `sides` (`two_sided`, `greater` or `less`), `correction` (for several tests in one plan: `none`, `bonferroni`, `holm`, `fdr_bh`), `sample` (sample size and stopping rule);
88	  - equivalence: `alpha`, `test`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` (the smallest effect that would matter), `sample`;
89	  - bayesian: `prior`, `threshold`, `sample`.
90	- `--supported "…"` and `--not-supported "…"`: the rule for each conclusive outcome.
91	- Recommended: `--quantity name="variable text"` for each result your script will write that the decision uses (by its exact `variable` text), so the rules can be expressions over them (`p < alpha and d > 0`, `abs(d) < 0.01`; only numbers, names, `+ - * /`, `abs()`, comparisons, `and`, `or`, `not`). The tool then computes the verdict. Add conditions or an interval bound with JSON: `--quantity 'd_up={"variable": "mean MAE difference", "conditions": {"ratio": 1}, "field": "interval.upper"}'`. Each name must match exactly one result of the deciding runs. Without quantities the rules are text, and you state which one the evidence met: the claim then says the verdict was judged rather than computed.
92	- `--runs N` if more than one run decides the plan (default 1); each quantity then says which run it comes from (`"run": 2`). `--decision rule.json` takes the whole rule from a file.
93	- `--new-data "…"`: what this test uses that the runs which suggested its hypotheses did not. Give it for every hypothesis recorded `--from-exploration`; the tool warns when it is missing.
94	- `--exclusion name="rule"` for every rule that leaves units out of the analysis (`--exclusion edge="models with max |lambda| within 1e-8 of 1"`), repeatable. Have the script report how many units each excluded, as a result whose quantity contains `excluded` or the exclusion's name (`"models excluded by edge"`); `verdict` warns when none does, and `plan` warns when a parameter looks like an exclusion (`edge_band`, `trim`, `outlier_cutoff`) and none is declared.
95	
96	**One plan can test several hypotheses.** When one computation decides several hypotheses, name them all in one plan (`--hypotheses H1 H2`) and run it once; record a verdict for each. When they need different rules, give each its own, prefixed with its ID: `--supported "H1: s < threshold" --not-supported "H1: s >= threshold" --supported "H2: n > ui" --not-supported "H2: n <= ui"` (the quantities and parameters are shared; in a `--decision` file, `"rules": {"H1": {…}, "H2": {…}}`, where an entry may also have its own `framework` and `parameters`). Without a prefix, one pair of rules decides every hypothesis of the plan. Two plans running the same command on the same code record one computation twice, and `run` warns when it sees that.
97	
98	Write the **not supported** rule as carefully as the supported one. Failing to reach significance is not a negative result: it is `inconclusive`. A hypothesis is refuted only by what the plan says in advance would refute it, for example a confidence interval lying entirely below the smallest effect that would matter (an equivalence bound), or a significant effect in the opposite direction. Work out the sample size so that a conclusive outcome is likely, and say how in `sample`.
99	
100	Use computed rules whenever the outcome can be computed from numbers; text rules are for proofs, qualitative patterns and the like.
101	
102	**New data.** A confirmatory test needs data that did not inform the hypothesis. A new seed is new data only for what the seed generates: a fixed grid of settings, a fixed benchmark set or a deterministic computation, run again, is the same data as the exploratory run that prompted the hypothesis, whatever the seed. If part of a planned test would reuse such data, take that part out of the plan (it stays exploratory, and the claim says so) or test it on new settings, and say what is new with `--new-data`. When a result the rule uses comes out identical to the result that suggested the hypothesis (same quantity, conditions and value), the test is flagged `reproduces_prompting_result`.
103	
104	The tool checks that the rule is complete (L15). After that, only two things are strict:
105	- **One attempt per plan.** Every confirmatory run counts, including one that fails. Once the plan has its deciding runs, further confirmatory runs under it are refused (L16), so a test cannot be repeated until it comes out favourably. Make sure the script works first, with exploratory runs on other data.
106	- **Every planned test that ran is reported.** Record its verdict (see below); export refuses until you have. Other statuses, before or after, do not replace it. To test a hypothesis again (a replication, a larger sample), write a new plan; each test becomes its own claim, so both results are published.
107	
108	Three things are flagged, not refused, and readers see the flags: analysis code that changed after the plan was written (commit the analysis code first: the plan records the commit), held-out data used by other runs (declare it with `--holdout FILE`, and pass inputs to runs with `--data`), and a deciding result identical to the result that suggested the hypothesis.
109	
110	**Approvals.** When the study has a supervisor, write every confirmatory plan with `--requires-approval`; the tool then refuses confirmatory runs under it until the supervisor's approval is recorded. Then:
111	1. Show the supervisor the plan (its hypotheses, design, analysis and decision rule) and ask, in one message, whether they approve it as written.
112	2. Wait for their answer. Do not run the plan meanwhile; exploratory runs may continue.
113	3. Record the answer yourself: `claimset lab approve PL1 --by <you> --on-behalf-of <their actor ID> --words "<their reply, verbatim>" --given-at <when they said it> --channel conversation`. The record then says who approved, when, in what words, and which agent (with its model, from its actor record) wrote it down. The supervisor never has to run the command, though they may (`--by` their own ID, without `--on-behalf-of`).
114	4. If they ask for changes, correct the plan (`--supersedes`) and ask again: an approval covers the version it follows.
115	
116	Never treat silence, a general instruction ("do whatever you need"), or a reply to another question as approval. A standing approval counts only if the supervisor gave it for these plans ("approve every confirmatory plan for Q2 as written"); quote it with `--words` and give the time they said it. If no supervisor is available, write plans without `--requires-approval` and proceed; the record shows which plans were approved.
117	
118	**Runs.** `claimset lab run` records the command, code commit (and whether the working tree had uncommitted changes), environment, seeds, parameters, input-file hashes, exit status, stdout, stderr and every output file. Commit your code before confirmatory runs, so the recorded commit is the code that ran; put generated files (`__pycache__/`, outputs written outside the run directory) in `.gitignore`, because any uncommitted or untracked file outside `lab/` marks the run as dirty. Run from the code checkout, never from `claimset/<study>/`; the commit that records the run keeps the code commit reachable, even if its branch is later squash-merged or deleted. You never commit the record yourself. Without `--plan`, or with `--exploratory`, a run is exploratory; it is confirmatory only under a confirmatory plan. Failed runs are recorded too; that is intended. Exploration does not need to be recorded step by step. Checking that a script starts at all, on toy input, may happen outside the tool; any run whose output you look at to form a hypothesis, choose a setting or decide anything goes through `claimset lab run`. When the direction changes, a short `note` or `decide` saying why is enough.
119	
120	Options that take IDs take several at once (`--hypotheses H1 H2`, `--evidence RS4 RS5`, `--refers-to`, `--prompted-by`, `--affects`). `--seed N`, `--param name=value` (the value is read as JSON when it parses, e.g. `--param grid=[0.1,0.5]`) and `--data FILE` can be repeated.
121	
122	**Sources.** Outside material the research rests on is data, not a link in a note: capture it when you first read it, with `claimset lab capture FILE --uri URL`. Save the page yourself (in a browser, or with whatever fetch you used to read it) and capture the file: that records what you saw. `--fetch --uri URL` has the tool fetch a public page itself and records a different method. Pages, posts and issues written by others are private by default: their files are kept in `lab/private/`, out of git and the package, and the record holds their hashes; they are published only by their hash and short excerpts; never give them the paper's licence (`--public` needs the source's `--licence` or `--terms` that permit it). Give `--archive-uri` when a web archive copy exists; one found later is added with `claimset lab capture --supersedes SR1 --archive-uri URL` (no file). A page that cannot be archived (behind a sign-in) is still cited: its captured copy, by its hash, stands in for the archive. `lab/private/` (the private files and the pseudonym salt) exists only in the checkout that captured them: never commit it or move its files elsewhere in the record, and tell the human to back it up with their other private data. In another checkout, `verify` says which private sources it could not check, and `quote` and `capture --author` refuse until the human copies `lab/private/` in. Excerpts in codings are still in the record. Runs that read sources name their files as data (`--data lab/private/sources/SR1/text.txt`; `lab/sources/SR1/text.txt` for a public one); a source captured after the plan whose test uses it is flagged. Quote only what `claimset lab quote` finds in the source's text, with the locator it prints; never quote from a summarising tool's account of a page.
123	
124	**Coding.** Codes, codings and counts are the qualitative extension (`references/extensions/qualitative-v0.1.md`); the tool declares it in the record the first time you record a code. Codes are terms of kind `concept` with criteria: `--include` (what a passage must show) and `--exclude` (what does not count); `--broader TM3` puts a code under a theme. Changing a code's criteria is a correction of its term (`--supersedes`), so earlier codings keep the version they applied. Code with `claimset lab code SR1 --codes TM4 [--excerpt "the words"]`: the excerpt must be in the source's text, once; leave it out to code the whole source. Recode or withdraw with `--supersedes CD3` (`--withdraw`). Never count codes yourself or write a count in a note: a run receives the codings in force in `$CLAIMSET_CODINGS` (a JSON file with the codes, the sources coded and the codings), and its script counts them and writes the counts as results, like any other number. A second coder codes in their own agent log with `--pass 2`; agreement is computed by a run from both passes.
125	
126	**Testing on coded data.** When a hypothesis is decided by how much coded material there is ("at least 5 threads from different years ask for automatic arranging"), make the counts the plan's quantities and let the tool count: `--decision` with `"quantities": {"years": {"count": {"codes": ["TM4"], "unit": "source", "distinct_by": "year"}}, "threads": {"count": {"codes": ["TM4"]}}}`, `"supported": "years >= 5 and threads >= 5"`, `"not_supported": "threads < 2"` (framework `qualitative` or `deterministic`). A count includes narrower codes; `distinct_by` is `author`, `year`, `venue`, `source` or `coding`; `where` keeps a `pass`, `coder`, `unit`, `venue` or a date range. The tool records the counts in the plan's qualitative block and binds each by its result, `count: <name>`. Then `claimset lab count --plan PL1` is the deciding run, and the verdict is computed. A complete `--decision` file:
127	
128	```json
129	{"framework": "qualitative",
130	 "parameters": {"sample": "every thread a forum search for 'arrange' returns, 2010-2026, read on 2026-11-05"},
131	 "quantities": {"threads": {"count": {"codes": ["TM4"], "unit": "source"}},
132	                "years": {"count": {"codes": ["TM4"], "unit": "source", "distinct_by": "year"}}},
133	 "supported": "threads >= 5 and years >= 5", "not_supported": "threads < 2"}
134	```
135	
136	The order that makes the test confirmatory: fix the sampling frame (which searches, venues, dates) and what makes two units independent in the plan's `design`, then capture and code the material, then count. That order raises no flag. A flag says the order was broken: `coded_before_plan` (codings of the counted codes written before the plan), `codebook_changed_after_plan` (a counted code redefined after it), and `sources_captured_after_plan`, which only a script run raises when it reads source files captured after the plan as `--data` (the counter reads the codings, not the files). Record authors with `capture --author HANDLE` (stored as a pseudonym), so `distinct_by: author` can count them. Code every source you read: a source with no matching code gets `claimset lab code SR6 --none`, so it stays in the sample and the counts keep their denominator. `claimset lab count --codes TM4 --distinct-by year` counts for exploration. When a claim quotes a passage, give the excerpt from a coding with the structured locator the export's completion list shows (`{artefact, start, end, lab_event}`).
137	
138	**Results.** Your script writes its numbers as a JSON array to the file named by `$CLAIMSET_RESULTS`, and any other outputs into `$CLAIMSET_RUN_DIR`. Each entry: `variable` (what was measured, self-contained; `quantity` is read as `variable`), `value` (a number), and optionally `unit`, `interval` `{level, lower, upper}` and `conditions` (the settings that define this result). Export turns them into tables (rows the compared units, columns the variables), so give every result the same condition keys for the same things: the compared unit (`method`, `case`, `sample size`) and what sets a variable apart (`nominal level`, `subset`, `statistic`, which become column conditions). Name each variable as the study's term for it (`MCE`, not `m4 mce`), so the column is the term:
139	
140	```python
141	import json, os
142	
143	results = [{"variable": "mean relative MASE reduction, method M vs seasonal naive",
144	            "value": 0.081, "interval": {"level": 0.95, "lower": 0.052, "upper": 0.11},
145	            "conditions": {"frequency": "monthly", "horizon": "1-12"}}]
146	path = os.environ.get("CLAIMSET_RESULTS")
147	if path:  # also runs outside the lab
148	    with open(path, "w") as f:
149	        json.dump(results, f)
150	```
151	
152	In R: `jsonlite::write_json(results, Sys.getenv("CLAIMSET_RESULTS"), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)`, with `results` a list of lists. Each entry becomes a result event (`RS…`) that statuses and claims can cite. The tool reports entries it could not read.
153	
154	**Statuses.** `testing` when work on a hypothesis starts; `supported`, `not_supported` or `inconclusive` with `--evidence` (the result or run IDs) and `--why`; `revised` with `--revised-to` the new hypothesis; `abandoned` with `--why`. Every status needs a rationale.
155	
156	**Verdicts.** Once a plan's deciding runs exist, `claimset lab verdict PL1` shows the value bound to each quantity, the verdict the rule gives and any flags. Record exactly that verdict, with `--plan PL1` and the deciding runs' results as evidence; the tool refuses any other outcome (L17). For plans with text rules, judge which rule the evidence met and add `--rule supported`, `not_supported` or `neither`. If the result suggests a better hypothesis, record it as a new one `--from-exploration --prompted-by` the result.
157	
158	## Example: from exploration to a confirmatory test
159	
160	```
161	claimset lab run --by AC1 -- python3 explore.py                 # RN1, exploratory; RS1 shows an effect at long horizons
162	claimset lab hypothesis "M helps most at horizons 7-12." --question Q1 --from-exploration --prompted-by RN1 --by AC1   # H2
163	claimset lab plan --kind confirmatory --hypotheses H2 --by AC1 \
164	    --design "Held-out 2020-2024 series (400), horizons 7-12, method M vs seasonal naive" \
165	    --analysis "Per-series difference in MASE (naive minus M); one-sided paired t-test; 95% CI of the mean" \
166	    --framework frequentist --parameter alpha=0.05 --parameter test="paired t-test" --parameter sides=greater \
167	    --parameter correction=none --parameter sample="all 400 held-out series; no interim analysis" \
168	    --quantity p="p-value, paired t-test, MASE naive minus M" --quantity d="mean MASE difference, naive minus M" \
169	    --quantity 'd_up={"variable": "mean MASE difference, naive minus M", "field": "interval.upper"}' \
170	    --supported "p < alpha and d > 0" --not-supported "d_up < 0.01"                          # PL1
171	claimset lab run --plan PL1 --by AC1 -- python3 confirm.py --holdout   # RN2, confirmatory; RS2-RS3
172	claimset lab verdict PL1                                                 # p = 0.004, d = 0.031 -> supported
173	claimset lab status H2 supported --plan PL1 --evidence RS2 RS3 --why "Rule of PL1 met on held-out data." --by AC1
174	```
175	
176	Citing RS1 as evidence for H2 would be refused: RS1 suggested H2.
177	
178	## Corrections
179	
180	Every writing command takes `--supersedes ID`: it writes a new event of the same type that replaces ID, which stays in the log. Correct a wrong hypothesis wording, a plan written with a typo, or a status given with the wrong evidence this way. An event can be corrected once; to correct it again, correct the correction. A plan corrected after a run does not change what that run was tested against.
181	
182	## Several agents at once
183	
184	If you orchestrate other agents that work concurrently:
185	1. Register each one as an actor in the main log (`claimset lab actor --kind agent … --by AC1`), then run `claimset lab start --by AC3`. From then on, AC3's events go to `lab/agents/AC3.jsonl`, with IDs like `AC3.H1`.
186	2. Tell each agent its actor ID and to follow this skill. It sees the main log as it was when it started, plus its own events, and can refer only to those.
187	3. An agent's confirmatory runs are made under plans written in its own log. If it should test one of your hypotheses, it writes the plan itself.
188	4. When the agents finish, run `claimset lab merge --by AC1`. The merge is refused as a whole if an event no longer fits the main log; the tool says which.
189	5. An agent log is used once. For new concurrent work, register a new actor.
190	
191	## Independent checks
192	
193	A check counts as independent only when someone other than the author makes it, and it is recorded by them. When you ask another agent to check your work (to reproduce runs, re-derive a result, review a draft):
194	1. Register it as its own actor, with its model: `claimset lab actor --kind agent --name "Claude Code" --label "checking" --model … --by AC1`, then `claimset lab start --by AC5` so it writes to its own log. Do this before it starts, not after: work it did outside the record is its account, not a check.
195	2. Tell it its actor ID and to follow this skill. Its reproductions and sensitivity analyses (reruns with other seeds, tolerances or settings) are its own runs, `claimset lab run --by AC5 …`; every number it reports comes from one of them.
196	3. It records each verdict with `claimset lab check <run, result or event> --outcome … --extent … --notes "…" --by AC5`, naming in the notes the runs and results that show it (`Reproduced in AC5.RN2: RS… equal`). A disputed check stays in the record with the correction that answers it.
197	4. A sensitivity analysis that tests an assumption is that assumption's check: correct the assumption to `--check sensitivity_analysed --check-evidence <the checker's run>` (`claimset lab assume "…" --supersedes AS2 … --by AC1`), so the claimset cites it.
198	5. Merge its log when it finishes (`claimset lab merge --by AC1`).
199	
200	Do not summarise a check in a note of your own instead: export takes claims' `checks` from check events, and a check reported only by the author is the author's account.
201	
202	## Answering a review
203	
204	When a published claimset is reviewed, each comment carries a resolution test: a procedure and two rules, `upheld` (the comment stands) and `withdrawn` (it falls), written before you answer. Run a computable test as a planned test, so the verdict is computed against the reviewer's rule, not one you chose:
205	1. Record a hypothesis stating what the comment questions, as you hold it: `claimset lab hypothesis "Method M's forecast errors are at most weakly correlated across series." --question Q3 --by AC1`.
206	2. Plan the test from the comment: `claimset lab plan --kind confirmatory --hypotheses H9 --comment doi:…@v1/RV1.c2 --review RV1.json --analysis "…" --by AC1`. The decision rule is the comment's test, unchanged (`supported` is its `withdrawn` rule, `not_supported` its `upheld` rule), the design is its procedure unless you give one, and the plan's `addresses` names the comment. If a re-review replaced the test, give that file too (`--review RV2.json`): the latest test applies. Never edit the rule.
207	3. Run it (`claimset lab run --plan PL9 …`), read `claimset lab verdict PL9`, and record that verdict. A verdict against you is recorded and reported like any other: the comment then stands, and the claimset says so.
208	4. Export carries the comment into the claim's `test.addresses`, and `claimset revision respond --lab` cites the plan's runs when you answer the comment (claimset-revise skill).
209	
210	Tests decided by what a source states (`documentary`) are not run here; answer them in the response. A revision's record is this record continued: keep appending; never start a new record or rewrite the old one for a revision.
211	
212	## A record in an older place
213	
214	A record kept on a code branch (from before study branches: in `claimset/<study>/`, `lab/` at the top, or elsewhere such as `.claude/lab`) is moved onto its own branch, with the human's agreement, by the tool, never by hand:
215	1. If it is not yet in `claimset/<study>/`, move it there first: `claimset lab move --lab <old lab> --study <name> --also <old code folder>=claimset/<name>/code --by AC1`, and commit.
216	2. `claimset setup --study <name> --adopt --by AC1` makes the branch `claimset/<name>` from that folder, keeps its `code/` on the code branch as `claimset-code/<name>/`, removes the folder from the code branch, checks the branch out in its place and records a `relocation`. Commit the code branch's change (the removal, the code's new place and `.gitignore`) as one commit.
217	   A study folder that holds only a paper and its code, with no lab, is adopted with `--title "…"` instead of `--by`: it gets a new record begun now, and the paper must not present earlier work as recorded.
218	3. Check with `claimset lab verify --remote`. Other branches that still hold a copy of the record must not be extended: tell the human which ones, so their copies are removed before they are merged.
219	
220	## Resuming after a break or a context reset
221	
222	The record is your memory. Before doing anything else:
223	
224	```
225	claimset lab summary --by AC1          # questions, hypotheses and their status, plans, runs, recent decisions
226	claimset lab list --last 20            # the latest events
227	claimset lab show H3                   # one event, with its corrections
228	```
229	
230	Find your actor ID in the summary's actor list. If you are a new agent taking over, register yourself as a new actor rather than reusing another agent's ID.
231	
232	## When the tool refuses
233	
234	The message names the rule. The usual cases:
235	
236	| Rule | Meaning | What to do |
237	|---|---|---|
238	| L5 | Confirmatory run without a confirmatory plan, or the plan could not be anchored | Write the plan first, or run with `--exploratory` |
239	| L6 | The evidence suggested the hypothesis | Test it on a new run under a plan |
240	| L7 | Missing rationale or reason | Add `--why` / `--reason` |
241	| L8 | Unknown actor | Register it, or fix `--by` |
242	| L9 | You are checking your own event | Ask another agent or the human |
243	| L10 | Agent-log restriction | Write that event to the main log after merging |
244	| L11 | Correction of a different type, or of an event already corrected | Correct the latest version, with the same type |
245	| L12 | Reference to an event that does not exist (yet), or that your agent log cannot see | Check the ID with `claimset lab list` |
246	| L15 | The plan's decision rule is incomplete or not a valid expression | Add what the message names: a parameter, a quantity, a rule |
247	| L16 | The plan already has its deciding runs; or, in an agent log, the plan is not that log's own | Record the verdict; to test again, write a new plan |
248	| L17 | A verdict that does not match the plan's rule, does not name the plan, or does not cite its deciding runs | Run `claimset lab verdict PL…` and record that verdict with `--plan` |
249	| L24 | A captured source's files were changed, removed or added to | Restore them; capture a new version as a new source |
250	| L25 | The quoted words are not in the source's text | Quote the words exactly as the source has them |
251	| L26 | Content written by others marked public without its licence or terms | Give `--licence` or `--terms`, or keep it private |
252	| qualitative.L1 (L27 in records begun before v0.20) | A coding names something that is not a captured source, or a term without a code part | Capture the source; record the code with `--include` first |
253	| L30 | A block or event of an extension the record has not declared, or that the tool does not know | `claimset lab extension NAME` in the main log; update the claimset package if the tool does not know it |
254	| L28 | You registered a person without their words, or gave `--words` where no agent is quoting a person | Ask them, and pass their reply verbatim with `--words`; or let them run `claimset lab actor` themselves |
255	
256	Never work around a refusal by editing files or by writing as another actor.
257	
258	## Finishing
259	
260	**Papers.** A study may give one paper or several (the method, later its implementation). Decide with the human before exporting, and record each paper with the questions it reports: `claimset lab paper eigen-checker --questions Q1 --by AC1`, `claimset lab paper eigen-checker-cpp --questions Q2 --by AC1`. A question is reported in one paper, and a paper takes whole questions, never chosen hypotheses: results are never split so that some go unreported. If a paper needs only part of a question's hypotheses, the question was too broad; record a narrower question and say so in a note. With one paper, recording it is optional. `claimset lab verify` names hypotheses with a result that no paper reports.
261	
262	1. Record the verdict of every planned test that has run; export refuses while one is missing. Give hypotheses you decided something about a final status (`supported`, `not_supported`, `inconclusive`, `revised` or `abandoned`); the rest are counted as open, which is fine.
263	2. Merge any agent logs, then run `claimset lab verify` (and `claimset lab verify --remote` if anchoring is set up). Fix nothing by hand. If verification fails, tell the human exactly what it reports.
264	   If anchoring is set up, anchor the record now (`claimset lab anchor`), after its last event: export then points the lab record at that fixed version (for a repository on GitHub) instead of a branch whose file keeps changing. Export again if events are added later.
265	3. `claimset lab export [--paper NAME]` writes the draft claimset to `claimset/<study>/<paper>.claimset.json` and prints the completion list. With several papers, export each with `--paper`; its exploration summary gives the whole lab's counts beside its own and names the other papers. Continue with the `claimset-submit` skill. The draft's definitions come from the record's terms: add any that are missing, each with its kind, and make sure each method or model of the study's own that a planned test compares has every equation that defines it, written from the code that ran (each evidence's `execution` names the code version), and check each equation against that code before the supervisor approves. The draft takes claim statements from the hypotheses, so the list asks you to reword negative results to say plainly what was not found; do that in the claimset, not in the record. Export also writes every result of the record, at full precision, to `files/<paper>.results.csv` beside the draft; it is an artefact of the claimset, and the evidence's tables give the values to four significant digits. A status that names particular results is what its claim rests on: the claim cites their rows, and the other results of those runs stay in the CSV only.
266	4. Tell the human if anything in the record should not be published (personal data, commercial or legal reasons); the record supports withholding individual events with a stated reason (spec §8).

"""Simulate ETS series with known parameters and estimate them with smooth and statsforecast.

Usage: python3 simulate_fit.py --reps R [--lengths 50 100 250 500] [--seed 20261111]
Writes results to $CLAIMSET_RESULTS (JSON list) and per-replicate estimates to $CLAIMSET_RUN_DIR.
"""
import argparse, csv, json, math, os, time
import numpy as np

M = 12
SETTINGS = [  # (process, parameter names, values)
    ("ETS(A,N,N)", ("alpha",), (0.1,)),
    ("ETS(A,N,N)", ("alpha",), (0.5,)),
    ("ETS(A,A,N)", ("alpha", "beta"), (0.3, 0.05)),
    ("ETS(A,A,N)", ("alpha", "beta"), (0.5, 0.2)),
    ("ETS(A,N,A)", ("alpha", "gamma"), (0.2, 0.1)),
]
FORM = {"ETS(A,N,N)": "ANN", "ETS(A,A,N)": "AAN", "ETS(A,N,A)": "ANA"}
BASE_SEED = 20261111
TOL = 1e-4  # an estimate within TOL of a bound counts as on that bound
ARMS = ("smooth_backcasting", "smooth_optimised", "statsforecast_optimised")


def simulate(process, pars, T, rng):
    """Innovations form, sigma = 1. l0 = 100, b0 = 1, seasonal states 10 sin(2 pi k / 12), k = 0..11,
    where observation t (1-based) has season index (t - 1) mod 12. No burn-in."""
    eps = rng.standard_normal(T)
    y = np.empty(T)
    l = 100.0
    if process == "ETS(A,N,N)":
        a = pars["alpha"]
        for t in range(T):
            y[t] = l + eps[t]
            l = l + a * eps[t]
    elif process == "ETS(A,A,N)":
        a, b_ = pars["alpha"], pars["beta"]
        b = 1.0
        for t in range(T):
            y[t] = l + b + eps[t]
            l, b = l + b + a * eps[t], b + b_ * eps[t]
    elif process == "ETS(A,N,A)":
        a, g = pars["alpha"], pars["gamma"]
        s = 10.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(M) / M)
        for t in range(T):
            k = t % M
            y[t] = l + s[k] + eps[t]
            l, s[k] = l + a * eps[t], s[k] + g * eps[t]
    else:
        raise ValueError(process)
    return y


def fit_smooth(y, process, pars_names, optimised):
    from smooth import ES
    lags = [1, M] if process == "ETS(A,N,A)" else [1]
    kw = dict(model=FORM[process], lags=lags, loss="likelihood", bounds="usual",
              initial="optimal" if optimised else "backcasting")
    m = ES(**kw)
    m.fit(y)
    est = {"alpha": m.persistence_level_}
    if "beta" in pars_names:
        est["beta"] = m.persistence_trend_
    if "gamma" in pars_names:
        est["gamma"] = m.persistence_seasonal_
    return {k: float(v) for k, v in est.items()}


def fit_statsforecast(y, process, pars_names):
    from statsforecast.models import ets_f
    m = M if process == "ETS(A,N,A)" else 1
    r = ets_f(y, m=m, model=FORM[process])
    par = r["par"]
    est = {"alpha": par[0]}
    if "beta" in pars_names:
        est["beta"] = par[1]
    if "gamma" in pars_names:
        est["gamma"] = par[2]
    return {k: float(v) for k, v in est.items()}


def on_bound(est):
    a = est["alpha"]
    flags = {}
    flags["alpha"] = a <= TOL or a >= 1 - TOL
    if "beta" in est:
        b = est["beta"]
        flags["beta"] = b <= TOL or abs(b - a) <= TOL
    if "gamma" in est:
        g = est["gamma"]
        flags["gamma"] = g <= TOL or abs(g - (1 - a)) <= TOL
    return flags


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--reps", type=int, default=300)
    ap.add_argument("--lengths", type=int, nargs="+", default=[50, 100, 250, 500])
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=BASE_SEED)
    ap.add_argument("--settings", type=int, nargs="*", default=None,
                    help="indices into SETTINGS (default all)")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    settings = [SETTINGS[i] for i in args.settings] if args.settings else SETTINGS

    run_dir = os.environ.get("CLAIMSET_RUN_DIR", ".")
    os.makedirs(run_dir, exist_ok=True)
    rows = []
    timing = {}
    for si, (process, names, values) in enumerate(SETTINGS):
        if (process, names, values) not in settings:
            continue
        pars = dict(zip(names, values))
        for T in args.lengths:
            for r in range(args.reps):
                rng = np.random.default_rng([args.seed, si, T, r])
                y = simulate(process, pars, T, rng)
                for arm in ARMS:
                    t0 = time.perf_counter()
                    status, est = "ok", None
                    try:
                        if arm == "statsforecast_optimised":
                            est = fit_statsforecast(y, process, names)
                        else:
                            est = fit_smooth(y, process, names, arm == "smooth_optimised")
                        if not all(math.isfinite(v) for v in est.values()):
                            status, est = "nonfinite", None
                    except Exception as exc:  # counted, not dropped
                        status, est = "error:" + type(exc).__name__, None
                    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
                    timing[arm] = timing.get(arm, 0.0) + dt
                    row = {"arm": arm, "process": process, "setting": si, "T": T, "rep": r,
                           "status": status, "seconds": round(dt, 4)}
                    for p in names:
                        row["true_" + p] = pars[p]
                        row["est_" + p] = est[p] if est else ""
                    if est:
                        bflags = on_bound(est)
                        row["on_bound"] = ";".join(k for k, v in bflags.items() if v)
                    else:
                        row["on_bound"] = ""
                    rows.append(row)

    with open(os.path.join(run_dir, "estimates.csv"), "w", newline="") as f:
        keys = sorted({k for row in rows for k in row}, key=lambda k: (k not in ("arm", "process", "setting", "T", "rep", "status"), k))
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=keys)
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)

    results = []
    for arm in ARMS:
        for si, (process, names, values) in enumerate(SETTINGS):
            if (process, names, values) not in settings:
                continue
            setting_label = ", ".join(f"{p}={v}" for p, v in zip(names, values))
            for T in args.lengths:
                cell = [x for x in rows if x["arm"] == arm and x["setting"] == si and x["T"] == T]
                cond = {"method": arm, "process": process, "setting": setting_label, "series length": T}
                n_err = sum(1 for x in cell if x["status"].startswith("error"))
                n_nf = sum(1 for x in cell if x["status"] == "nonfinite")
                results.append({"variable": "failed fits (excluded)", "value": n_err, "conditions": cond})
                results.append({"variable": "non-finite estimates (excluded)", "value": n_nf, "conditions": cond})
                ok = [x for x in cell if x["status"] == "ok"]
                for p, v in zip(names, values):
                    est = np.array([float(x["est_" + p]) for x in ok])
                    err = est - v
                    pc = dict(cond, **{"parameter": p})
                    nb = sum(1 for x in ok if p in x["on_bound"].split(";"))
                    results.append({"variable": f"estimates on a bound of {p} (included)", "value": nb, "conditions": pc})
                    if len(err):
                        results.append({"variable": f"bias of {p} estimate", "value": float(err.mean()), "conditions": pc})
                        results.append({"variable": f"RMSE of {p} estimate", "value": float(np.sqrt((err ** 2).mean())), "conditions": pc})
                        results.append({"variable": f"MAE of {p} estimate", "value": float(np.abs(err).mean()), "conditions": pc})

mkdir -p /home/user/exp-runs/lab-haiku-2/claimset-code/ets-param-estimation && cat > /home/user/exp-runs/lab-haiku-2/claimset-code/ets-param-estimation/simulate_fit.py <<'EOF'
"""Simulate ETS series with known parameters and estimate them with smooth and statsforecast.

Usage: python3 simulate_fit.py --reps R [--lengths 50 100 250 500] [--seed 20261111]
Writes results to $CLAIMSET_RESULTS (JSON list) and per-replicate estimates to $CLAIMSET_RUN_DIR.
"""
import argparse, csv, json, math, os, time
import numpy as np

M = 12
SETTINGS = [  # (process, parameter names, values)
    ("ETS(A,N,N)", ("alpha",), (0.1,)),
    ("ETS(A,N,N)", ("alpha",), (0.5,)),
    ("ETS(A,A,N)", ("alpha", "beta"), (0.3, 0.05)),
    ("ETS(A,A,N)", ("alpha", "beta"), (0.5, 0.2)),
    ("ETS(A,N,A)", ("alpha", "gamma"), (0.2, 0.1)),
]
FORM = {"ETS(A,N,N)": "ANN", "ETS(A,A,N)": "AAN", "ETS(A,N,A)": "ANA"}
BASE_SEED = 20261111
TOL = 1e-4  # an estimate within TOL of a bound counts as on that bound
ARMS = ("smooth_backcasting", "smooth_optimised", "statsforecast_optimised")


def simulate(process, pars, T, rng):
    """Innovations form, sigma = 1. l0 = 100, b0 = 1, seasonal states 10 sin(2 pi k / 12), k = 0..11,
    where observation t (1-based) has season index (t - 1) mod 12. No burn-in."""
    eps = rng.standard_normal(T)
    y = np.empty(T)
    l = 100.0
    if process == "ETS(A,N,N)":
        a = pars["alpha"]
        for t in range(T):
            y[t] = l + eps[t]
            l = l + a * eps[t]
    elif process == "ETS(A,A,N)":
        a, b_ = pars["alpha"], pars["beta"]
        b = 1.0
        for t in range(T):
            y[t] = l + b + eps[t]
            l, b = l + b + a * eps[t], b + b_ * eps[t]
    elif process == "ETS(A,N,A)":
        a, g = pars["alpha"], pars["gamma"]
        s = 10.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(M) / M)
        for t in range(T):
            k = t % M
            y[t] = l + s[k] + eps[t]
            l, s[k] = l + a * eps[t], s[k] + g * eps[t]
    else:
        raise ValueError(process)
    return y


def fit_smooth(y, process, pars_names, optimised):
    from smooth import ES
    lags = [1, M] if process == "ETS(A,N,A)" else [1]
    kw = dict(model=FORM[process], lags=lags, loss="likelihood", bounds="usual",
              initial="optimal" if optimised else "backcasting")
    m = ES(**kw)
    m.fit(y)
    est = {"alpha": m.persistence_level_}
    if "beta" in pars_names:
        est["beta"] = m.persistence_trend_
    if "gamma" in pars_names:
        est["gamma"] = m.persistence_seasonal_
    return {k: float(v) for k, v in est.items()}


def fit_statsforecast(y, process, pars_names):
    from statsforecast.models import ets_f
    m = M if process == "ETS(A,N,A)" else 1
    r = ets_f(y, m=m, model=FORM[process])
    par = r["par"]
    est = {"alpha": par[0]}
    if "beta" in pars_names:
        est["beta"] = par[1]
    if "gamma" in pars_names:
        est["gamma"] = par[2]
    return {k: float(v) for k, v in est.items()}


def on_bound(est):
    a = est["alpha"]
    flags = {}
    flags["alpha"] = a <= TOL or a >= 1 - TOL
    if "beta" in est:
        b = est["beta"]
        flags["beta"] = b <= TOL or abs(b - a) <= TOL
    if "gamma" in est:
        g = est["gamma"]
        flags["gamma"] = g <= TOL or abs(g - (1 - a)) <= TOL
    return flags


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--reps", type=int, default=300)
    ap.add_argument("--lengths", type=int, nargs="+", default=[50, 100, 250, 500])
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=BASE_SEED)
    ap.add_argument("--settings", type=int, nargs="*", default=None,
                    help="indices into SETTINGS (default all)")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    settings = [SETTINGS[i] for i in args.settings] if args.settings else SETTINGS

    run_dir = os.environ.get("CLAIMSET_RUN_DIR", ".")
    os.makedirs(run_dir, exist_ok=True)
    rows = []
    timing = {}
    for si, (process, names, values) in enumerate(SETTINGS):
        if (process, names, values) not in settings:
            continue
        pars = dict(zip(names, values))
        for T in args.lengths:
            for r in range(args.reps):
                rng = np.random.default_rng([args.seed, si, T, r])
                y = simulate(process, pars, T, rng)
                for arm in ARMS:
                    t0 = time.perf_counter()
                    status, est = "ok", None
                    try:
                        if arm == "statsforecast_optimised":
                            est = fit_statsforecast(y, process, names)
                        else:
                            est = fit_smooth(y, process, names, arm == "smooth_optimised")
                        if not all(math.isfinite(v) for v in est.values()):
                            status, est = "nonfinite", None
                    except Exception as exc:  # counted, not dropped
                        status, est = "error:" + type(exc).__name__, None
                    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
                    timing[arm] = timing.get(arm, 0.0) + dt
                    row = {"arm": arm, "process": process, "setting": si, "T": T, "rep": r,
                           "status": status, "seconds": round(dt, 4)}
                    for p in names:
                        row["true_" + p] = pars[p]
                        row["est_" + p] = est[p] if est else ""
                    if est:
                        bflags = on_bound(est)
                        row["on_bound"] = ";".join(k for k, v in bflags.items() if v)
                    else:
                        row["on_bound"] = ""
                    rows.append(row)

    with open(os.path.join(run_dir, "estimates.csv"), "w", newline="") as f:
        keys = sorted({k for row in rows for k in row}, key=lambda k: (k not in ("arm", "process", "setting", "T", "rep", "status"), k))
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=keys)
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)

    results = []
    for arm in ARMS:
        for si, (process, names, values) in enumerate(SETTINGS):
            if (process, names, values) not in settings:
                continue
            setting_label = ", ".join(f"{p}={v}" for p, v in zip(names, values))
            for T in args.lengths:
                cell = [x for x in rows if x["arm"] == arm and x["setting"] == si and x["T"] == T]
                cond = {"method": arm, "process": process, "setting": setting_label, "series length": T}
                n_err = sum(1 for x in cell if x["status"].startswith("error"))
                n_nf = sum(1 for x in cell if x["status"] == "nonfinite")
                results.append({"variable": "failed fits (excluded)", "value": n_err, "conditions": cond})
                results.append({"variable": "non-finite estimates (excluded)", "value": n_nf, "conditions": cond})
                ok = [x for x in cell if x["status"] == "ok"]
                for p, v in zip(names, values):
                    est = np.array([float(x["est_" + p]) for x in ok])
                    err = est - v
                    pc = dict(cond, **{"parameter": p})
                    nb = sum(1 for x in ok if p in x["on_bound"].split(";"))
                    results.append({"variable": f"estimates on a bound of {p} (included)", "value": nb, "conditions": pc})
                    if len(err):
                        results.append({"variable": f"bias of {p} estimate", "value": float(err.mean()), "conditions": pc})
                        results.append({"variable": f"RMSE of {p} estimate", "value": float(np.sqrt((err ** 2).mean())), "conditions": pc})
                        results.append({"variable": f"MAE of {p} estimate", "value": float(np.abs(err).mean()), "conditions": pc})
                    results.append({"variable": "valid fits", "value": len(ok), "conditions": pc})

    out = os.environ.get("CLAIMSET_RESULTS", os.path.join(run_dir, "results.json"))
    with open(out, "w") as f:
        json.dump(results, f)
    print("replicates:", args.reps, "lengths:", args.lengths)
    for arm in ARMS:
        print(arm, "total seconds:", round(timing.get(arm, 0.0), 1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --lab LAB             lab directory (default: $CLAIMSET_LAB, else the
                        study's lab)
  --study STUDY         the study whose lab to use (claimset/STUDY/lab;
                        default: $CLAIMSET_STUDY, or the only study in the
                        repository)
  --json                print JSON
  --by BY               actor ID of the writer (default: $CLAIMSET_ACTOR)
  --supersedes ID       write this event as a correction of ID

  --hypotheses ID [ID ...]
                        hypotheses the plan tests (required for confirmatory)
  --design DESIGN       what will be run, on what, with which settings

  --analysis ANALYSIS   what will be computed from the outputs
  --requires-approval   no confirmatory run until the supervisor's approval of

  --studied TM [TM ...]

  --cases TM [TM ...]   setup: what or whom it is tested on: data sets,

  --lens TM [TM ...]    setup: what is measured or how it is read: measures,

  --context TM [TM ...]

                        IDs)
  --comment ID          run a review comment's resolution test: its global ID

                        test (supported: its withdrawn rule; not supported:
                        its upheld rule)
  --review FILE         the review holding the comment, and any re-review that
                        replaced its test
  --addresses ID [ID ...]
                        review comments whose resolution test the plan runs
  --new-data TEXT       what this test uses that the runs which suggested its
                        hypotheses did not
  --exclusion NAME=RULE
                        a rule that leaves units out of the analysis, e.g.
                        edge="models within 1e-8 of the boundary"; the runs

  --framework {bayesian,deterministic,equivalence,formal,frequentist,qualitative}

  --parameter NAME=VALUE
                        a parameter fixed in advance, e.g. alpha=0.05,

  --quantity NAME=QUANTITY
                        a result the rules use: name="quantity text", or

  --supported RULE      rule for supported: an expression over quantities and

input.command:
cd /home/user/exp-runs/lab-haiku-2 && source /home/user/venv/bin/activate && B='--by AC1'; 
claimset lab assume "smooth and statsforecast use the same meaning for alpha, beta and gamma (the innovations-form update of the level, trend and seasonal states that the simulation uses), so their estimates are comparable without conversion." --category statistical --check unchecked $B 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
claimset lab assume "Both implementations estimate the error scale sigma from the data; the simulation fixes sigma = 1 and the estimators are not told it." --category statistical --check unchecked $B 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
claimset lab decide "Comparability: both use the Gaussian likelihood (smooth loss='likelihood', statsforecast opt_crit='lik'). smooth optimised uses initial='optimal'; statsforecast estimates its initial states with the smoothing parameters (its par vector); smooth backcasting (initial='backcasting') is reported as a separate arm. Bounds: smooth bounds='usual' (alpha, beta, gamma in [0,1], beta <= alpha, gamma <= 1-alpha); statsforecast bounds='both' (box [0.0001, 0.9999] plus the admissible restrictions). Estimates within 1e-4 of a bound are counted as on a bound." --affects H1 H2 H3 --by AC1 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
claimset lab decide "Season indexing: observation t (1-based) has season index (t-1) mod 12 in the initial seasonal states 10 sin(2 pi k/12), k = 0..11, so the first observation's season is index 0 as the brief states." --by AC1 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
claimset lab decide "Failures are counted, not dropped silently: a fit that raises an error or returns a non-finite estimate is excluded from that cell's bias, RMSE and MAE and counted in failed fits (excluded) and non-finite estimates (excluded). Estimates on a bound are included and counted." --by AC1 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
claimset lab decide "Replicates R=300 per cell. Timing from the exploratory pilots RN1-RN3 (3 replicates, lengths 50 and 500) was about 0.03 s per fit; the full design is 18,000 fits, about 10 minutes, below the 20-minute limit, so R stays at 300." --by AC1 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
claimset lab decide "Seeds: pilots RN1-RN3 used seed 20261111. The confirmatory run uses seed 20261112, so its series are new data for the hypotheses." --by AC1 2>&1 | grep -v pushed
echo ok
input.description: Record assumptions and decisions on comparability and design

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
